\section{Comparison with PPI Correction}
\label{app:ppi_comparison}

PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi} constructs confidence intervals by combining a large set of ML predictions with a smaller set of gold-standard labels, using the gold labels to debias the ML-based estimator.
Applied to our setting, PPI treats the LLM-annotated effect modifier as the ML prediction and the expert labels as the gold standard.
Two variants arise naturally: \emph{PPI-global} pools all expert labels to estimate a single rectifier (analogous to our Global baseline), and \emph{PPI-subgroup} estimates per-subgroup rectifiers (analogous to Stratified MLE).
The key difference from confusion-matrix inversion is that PPI does not invert the confusion matrix; instead, it uses the gold labels to directly debias the estimand.
This avoids the matrix inversion step that can amplify noise at small $n_{\text{expert}}$, but it also means PPI cannot exploit the structure of the misclassification process to reduce bias as aggressively.

Table~\ref{tab:ppi_comparison} compares PPI-global, PPI-subgroup, and EC-HTE under the synthetic DGP with extreme misclassification heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi = 0.20$, $\Delta\tau = 0.5$).
Three patterns emerge.
First, EC-HTE's hierarchical partial pooling consistently improves over Stratified MLE, confirming the value of borrowing strength across subgroups.
Second, all stratified correction methods incur a variance cost at $K{=}4$ with small $n_{\text{expert}}$, where RMSE exceeds Global correction---consistent with the crossover analysis in Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval} ($n_{\text{expert}} = 1{,}000$ for $K{=}4$).
Third, EC-HTE's primary value is bias correctness: it avoids the ``debiasing hurts'' failure mode (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) where global correction amplifies bias in low-error subgroups, whereas PPI-global inherits the same $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ bias amplification as Global correction regardless of the inference framework.
[Results for $K{=}2$ at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$, where EC-HTE is expected to achieve the RMSE crossover, will be added upon completion.]

\centering
\caption{PPI vs.\ EC-HTE comparison under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$, $\Delta\pi = 0.20$, $\Delta\tau = 0.5$). $|\text{Bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage averaged over subgroups and 100 MC runs. [PLACEHOLDER: awaiting experimental results]}
\label{tab:ppi_comparison}
\small
\begin{tabular}{ll ccc}

PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi} constructs confidence intervals by combining a large set of ML predictions with a smaller set of gold-standard labels, using the gold labels to debias the ML-based estimator.
Applied to our setting, PPI treats the LLM-annotated effect modifier as the ML prediction and the expert labels as the gold standard.
Two variants arise naturally: \emph{PPI-global} pools all expert labels to estimate a single rectifier (analogous to our Global baseline), and \emph{PPI-subgroup} estimates per-subgroup rectifiers (analogous to Stratified MLE).

Under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, DSL's measurement error correction reduces to confusion matrix inversion.
Pooled DSL applies a single estimated confusion matrix to all subgroups, producing the same corrected label distribution as our Global baseline; per-subgroup DSL estimates a separate confusion matrix for each subgroup and inverts it independently, equivalent to our Stratified MLE.
EC-HTE's contribution over both PPI-subgroup and per-subgroup DSL is hierarchical partial pooling: rather than estimating each subgroup's confusion matrix in isolation, EC-HTE places a shared prior across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance while preserving subgroup-specific bias correction.
This mechanism is outside both the PPI and DSL frameworks.

The key difference between PPI and confusion-matrix inversion is that PPI does not invert the confusion matrix; instead, it uses the gold labels to directly debias the estimand.
This avoids the matrix inversion step that can amplify noise at small $n_{\text{expert}}$, but it also means PPI cannot exploit the structure of the misclassification process to reduce bias.
PPI-global inherits the same $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ bias amplification as Global correction (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}), confirming that the ``debiasing hurts'' mechanism operates regardless of the inference framework.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The Director is orchestrating final-stage polish patches for the EC-HTE EMNLP 2026 Long Paper submission (DDL May 25, ~3 days away). This session covers multiple sequential Patch-mode edits:
   - Conclusion polish + coverage insight + Ogburn & VanderWeele citation
   - Writing optimization (保3.5冲4): real-data gap framing, diagnostic independent value, writing quality
   - Reviewer-driven relocation of validation framing from Limitations to Related Work
   - PPI/DSL baseline comparison (Task B): draft → hold → framing adjustment → finalize
   All patches follow: edit → compile with `paper_compile_and_check` → verify 0 critical + main text ≤ 8 pages → report via `paper_agent_post_to_director`.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - EC-HTE: Hierarchical Bayesian subgroup-stratified confusion matrix correction + CausalForestDML
   - Bias Decomposition Identity (Theorem 1): exact population-level identity, R²=0.994 (K=2)
   - Proposition 2 (Δτ-free diagnostic): |δ_s|/((1-2π̄)·π_s) > 1; subgroup-level AUC=0.86, setting-level AUC=0.89
   - DSL equivalence: Under confusion-matrix parameterization, pooled DSL = Global baseline, per-subgroup DSL = Stratified MLE; EC-HTE adds hierarchical partial pooling (outside DSL framework)
   - PPI vs CM-inversion: PPI directly debiases estimand without matrix inversion; PPI-global inherits Δπ×Δτ bias amplification
   - Coverage gain: 0.71 → 0.94 in multi-LLM validation
   - Ogburn & VanderWeele (2012): nondifferential confounder misclassification attenuates effects; our setting differs (effect modifier, correction can amplify)
   - EMNLP 2026: 8-page main text limit, unlimited references/limitations/appendix
   - Key numbers in current files: |bias| 0.010 (not 0.011), AUC 0.86 (not 0.87), 5.9× reduction (K=2)

3. Files and Code Sections:
   - **`conclusion.tex`**
     - Heavily compressed from 18 lines to 4 sentences to fit 8-page limit
     - Contains coverage insight: "the coverage gain (0.71 → 0.94) matters because undercovering intervals produce false confidence in spurious effects"
     - Current full content:
     ```latex
     \section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
     
     We proved an exact bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): global confusion-matrix correction introduces subgroup-level bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$, worsening CATE estimates in 50\% of configurations.
     EC-HTE addresses this via hierarchical Bayesian subgroup-stratified correction with a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}; AUC $= 0.86$); composed with PPCI, it reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007.
     The workflow requires only a pilot sample: check $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$ and apply EC-HTE ($n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$ for $K{=}2$, $\geq 1{,}000$ for $K{=}4$) when triggered; otherwise global correction suffices.
     EC-HTE's advantage is conditional---the coverage gain (0.71 $\to$ 0.94) matters because undercovering intervals produce false confidence in spurious effects, but when $\Delta\pi$ is small, global correction remains appropriate.
     ```

   - **`related_work.tex`**
     - Added Ogburn & VanderWeele citation (line 7)
     - Replaced DSL description with explicit equivalence statement + qualifier (line 21-22)
     - Added validation positioning at end (line 27)
     - Current PPI/DSL paragraph (lines 19-27):
     ```latex
     \paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
     PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
     In our setting---binary effect modifier with known subgroup structure, a special case of the broader problems DSL addresses---DSL's measurement error correction reduces, under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}).
     EC-HTE adds hierarchical partial pooling across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance---a mechanism outside the DSL framework.
     ...
     Our validation strategy---synthetic DGPs, a semi-synthetic experiment, and real LLM confusion matrices---is consistent with the evaluation methodology in PPI and DSL...
     ```

   - **`abstract.tex`**
     - Diagnostic reframed: "a computable diagnostic (AUC $= 0.86$) identifies when global correction increases bias from per-subgroup misclassification rates alone, actionable without adopting EC-HTE."

   - **`introduction.tex`**
     - Line 17: diagnostic "independently useful even without adopting EC-HTE"
     - Contributions item 1: "independently actionable without EC-HTE"

   - **`limitations.tex`**
     - Removed 3-sentence defensive validation paragraph (was L20-22)
     - Added forward-looking sentence (L19): "We leave full real-data validation---on a dataset combining RCT design, ground-truth CATEs, and LLM annotations---to future work as suitable public benchmarks become available."
     - 19 lines total, ~5 core points

   - **`appendix.tex`** (PPI comparison section, `app:ppi_comparison`)
     - Was being finalized when summary requested
     - Rewrote to remove placeholder table and RMSE comparison claims
     - New content: DSL equivalence proof (pooled DSL = Global, per-subgroup DSL = Strat MLE), EC-HTE's partial pooling contribution, PPI vs CM-inversion distinction, PPI-global inherits Δπ×Δτ bias
     - Final version (just written, not yet compiled):
     ```latex
     \section{Comparison with PPI Correction}
     \label{app:ppi_comparison}
     
     PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi} constructs confidence intervals by combining a large set of ML predictions with a smaller set of gold-standard labels...
     Two variants arise naturally: \emph{PPI-global}... and \emph{PPI-subgroup}...
     
     Under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, DSL's measurement error correction reduces to confusion matrix inversion.
     Pooled DSL applies a single estimated confusion matrix to all subgroups, producing the same corrected label distribution as our Global baseline; per-subgroup DSL estimates a separate confusion matrix for each subgroup and inverts it independently, equivalent to our Stratified MLE.
     EC-HTE's contribution over both PPI-subgroup and per-subgroup DSL is hierarchical partial pooling...
     
     The key difference between PPI and confusion-matrix inversion is that PPI does not invert the confusion matrix...
     PPI-global inherits the same $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ bias amplification as Global correction (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity})...
     ```

   - **`references.bib`**
     - Added `ogburn2012nondifferential` entry (Epidemiology, 2012, 23(3):433-439)

4. Errors and fixes:
   - **Page overflow (CRITICAL, multiple iterations)**: Adding coverage insight + forward-looking sentences to Conclusion + Ogburn sentence to Related Work pushed main text to page 9. Fix: (a) dropped forward-looking sentence per Director priority, (b) aggressive Conclusion compression (merged sentences, removed "This conditionality" redundant sentence, removed validation/future-work paragraph), (c) compressed Ogburn sentence. Required 4 compile-check cycles.
   - **Defensive framing in Limitations (Reviewer feedback)**: Director/Reviewer said "follows and extends the standard" in Limitations reads as deflecting criticism. \section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Measurement error and annotation models.}
Classical measurement error theory shows that correction via estimated error models can amplify MSE when the error structure is misspecified~\cite{fuller1987measurement,carroll2006measurement}; Bayesian approaches require informative priors when identification is weak~\cite{gustafson2003measurement}, and nonparametric methods use repeated measurements or instruments to recover the true distribution~\cite{hu2008nonparametric}.
We formalize this principle for a specific causal estimand: Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} gives an exact identity for CATE bias under global correction with heterogeneous misclassification.
\citet{ogburn2012nondifferential} show nondifferential confounder misclassification attenuates effects; our setting differs---the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier, and correction can amplify bias.
\citet{battistin2014treatment} study treatment effect estimation with covariate measurement error but focus on average effects rather than subgroup-level heterogeneity; \citet{fong2021machine} analyze error propagation when ML predictions serve as regression covariates but do not address the effect modifier setting.
In the annotation literature, \citet{dawid1979maximum} introduced confusion matrix estimation for multiple annotators, with extensions to item difficulty, annotator competence, and hierarchical priors~\cite{passonneau2014benefits,hovy2013learning,paun2018comparing}.
Our hierarchical estimator (Section~\ref{sec:method}) adapts this architecture from label aggregation to causal inference, tying the prior structure to the subgroup dimension that defines treatment effect heterogeneity.

\paragraph{HTE estimation and LLM annotation error.}
Causal forests~\cite{athey2016recursive,wager2018causal}, double/debiased ML~\cite{chernozhukov2018dml}, doubly-robust CATE estimators~\cite{kennedy2023dr}, and meta-learners~\cite{kunzel2019metalearners} all assume that covariates defining heterogeneity are observed without error; when the effect modifier is misclassified, CATE estimates conflate effects across groups.
EC-HTE provides upstream correction that restores valid inputs to any downstream estimator.
The corrected pseudo-outcomes are in principle compatible with other HTE estimators such as the R-learner~\citep{nie2021quasi}.
LLMs now match crowd-worker accuracy on many classification tasks~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp,pangakis2023automated}, but \citet{ashwin2025bias} show that error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups.
This subgroup-varying error is the failure mode we address: it distorts the very contrasts that define the research question, and prior work documents the pattern without providing a correction mechanism for downstream causal estimands.

\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
In our setting---binary effect modifier with known subgroup structure, a special case of the broader problems DSL addresses---DSL's measurement error correction reduces, under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}).
EC-HTE adds hierarchical partial pooling across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance---a mechanism outside the DSL framework.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification, requiring instrumental variables or partial identification; our problem is structurally distinct because the treatment is observed correctly but the effect modifier is misclassified, admitting exact correction through confusion matrices rather than bounds.
Extended discussion of these distinctions appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.
Our validation strategy---synthetic DGPs, a semi-synthetic experiment, and real LLM confusion matrices---is consistent with the evaluation methodology in PPI and DSL, which similarly rely on synthetic and semi-synthetic settings where ground-truth quantities are known by construction; Section~\ref{sec:multilm_opensource} supplements this with confusion matrices from four open-source LLMs, confirming that $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity arises in practice.

\section*{Limitations}

EC-HTE requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup for stable hierarchical Bayesian estimation.
For $K{=}2$, EC-HTE remains effective even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$ (Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}); for $K{=}4$, $P(Z{=}1) \geq 0.3$ is needed to approach breakeven with global correction at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$.
Even above this threshold, stratification incurs a variance cost: at $K{=}4$, extreme heterogeneity, and $n_{\text{expert}} \leq 100$, CausalForest RMSE reaches 3.5$\times$ that of the naive estimator.
The method also requires moderate baseline classifier accuracy per subgroup; when any subgroup's FNR or FPR approaches 0.5, the confusion matrix row approaches a uniform distribution and inversion amplifies noise (Appendix~\ref{app:semireal}), as confirmed independently in the hate speech case study (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}).
Additionally, our main semi-synthetic experiments use constant treatment effects across subgroups; a supplementary heterogeneous-$\tau$ DGP (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm_opensource}) shows that EC-HTE achieves targeted bias and RMSE improvement in subgroups with large $\Delta\tau$, though aggregate RMSE remains comparable to global correction.
Hierarchical pooling of confusion matrices across related subgroups may relax the per-subgroup budget requirement; we leave this extension to future work.

The variance-adjusted CausalForest uses a plug-in approximation: it propagates outcome uncertainty through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ but does not propagate confusion matrix estimation uncertainty itself.
This is reasonable at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$ but may understate total uncertainty below this threshold; full Bayesian propagation is left to future work.

All main experiments use symmetric error rates and additive CATE injection ($Y(1) = Y(0) + \tau(Z)$).
The bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) generalizes to asymmetric confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}, $R^2 = 0.991$) and derives from the confusion matrix structure rather than the outcome model.
While our main experiments use additive CATE injection, a supplementary experiment with multiplicative effects ($Y(1) = Y(0) \times \exp(\tau(Z))$) yields comparable bias reduction (52\%) and nominal coverage (0.955; Appendix~\ref{app:rlearner}), confirming robustness to the functional form of treatment effects.
EC-HTE further requires discrete, pre-defined subgroups; continuous effect modifiers or latent subgroup discovery settings require different approaches, and intersectional subgroups with many levels may exceed the $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ budget threshold.
Our experiments define subgroups by text features (hashtag presence, text length); demographic subgroups---where prior work documents the most concerning disparities \citep{ashwin2025bias}---require sensitive data access beyond the scope of this study.
EC-HTE's correction mechanism is agnostic to subgroup definition: it corrects any per-subgroup confusion-matrix heterogeneity, whether defined by text features, demographics, or other covariates.
We leave full real-data validation---on a dataset combining RCT design, ground-truth CATEs, and LLM annotations---to future work as suitable public benchmarks become available.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
Yet these annotations are not uniformly accurate.
\citet{ashwin2025bias} document that LLM misclassification rates vary by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level.
In a pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% binary accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$), within the range assumed in our synthetic DGPs ($\Delta\pi = 0.05$--$0.20$).
When such annotations serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, subgroup-specific errors propagate directly into conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
The resulting bias is not random noise that averages out; it is structured by the same demographic axes that define the research question.
Standard correction procedures, which estimate a single confusion matrix and apply its inverse uniformly, cannot account for this heterogeneity.

We formalize this problem and discover a previously unrecognized bias mechanism.
When a pooled confusion matrix is applied to correct subgroup CATEs, it misattributes error across subgroups with an exact product form: the bias in subgroup $s$ equals $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$, where $\delta_s$ is the deviation from the pooled error rate and $\Delta\tau$ is the CATE heterogeneity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}).
This is not a bound but an exact population-level identity, verified empirically with $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $R^2 = 0.974$ ($K{=}4$).
A direct consequence is that global correction can be worse than no correction at all: in 50\% of our experimental configurations, global correction increases absolute bias relative to the naive estimator, with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest).
Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE) addresses this through hierarchical Bayesian estimation of subgroup-stratified confusion matrices combined with CausalForestDML, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.010 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$).
The bias decomposition identity also yields a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction will increase bias (AUC = 0.86)---independently useful even without adopting EC-HTE, since practitioners can flag harmful correction from a pilot sample before estimating any treatment effects.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, global correction suffices and EC-HTE's variance cost is not justified (Figure~\ref{fig:bias_mechanism}).

This problem matters because subgroup CATEs inform resource allocation decisions: which communities benefit most from policy interventions, where programs should be targeted, and how reforms affect different groups.
Biased CATE estimates can reverse the sign of apparent treatment heterogeneity, leading practitioners to allocate resources away from communities that benefit most.
The failure mode is subtle: a researcher who corrects for annotation noise using a pooled confusion matrix may introduce more bias than doing nothing, precisely in the low-error subgroups where original labels were most trustworthy.
As LLM annotation pipelines replace manual coding across the social sciences, heterogeneous classification errors will propagate to an increasing share of causal analyses.

Several methods address measurement error in downstream statistical analyses, but none handles the specific failure mode we identify.
Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI;~\citealt{angelopoulos2023ppi}) and Design-based Supervised Learning~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates by combining predicted and gold-standard labels, assuming homogeneous prediction error across subgroups.
These methods produce valid confidence intervals for marginal quantities but do not extend to subgroup-conditional estimands.
Prediction-Powered Conditional Inference (PPCI;~\citealt{sui2026ppci}) extends PPI to conditional means but targets outcome-side prediction error rather than covariate-side misclassification; it corrects $\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$, not the reverse.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} prove that arm-specific rectifiers fix average treatment effect bias under differential prediction error, but their analysis is limited to population averages and does not address heterogeneity estimation.
ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} handles ML-covariate measurement error in regression forests but targets the outcome model rather than the treatment effect heterogeneity structure.
The gap is specific: no existing method corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the one that defines the heterogeneity structure itself, i.e., the effect modifier whose levels index the CATE function.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_bias_mechanism.pdf}
\caption{Bias mechanism under global vs.\ subgroup-stratified correction. Global correction applies the pooled error rate $\bar{\pi}$ uniformly, over-correcting low-error subgroups (introducing bias where none existed) and under-correcting high-error subgroups. EC-HTE matches each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification rate.}
\label{fig:bias_mechanism}
\end{figure}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) proving that global correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$, with a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}; AUC $= 0.86$) that flags when correction is harmful using only per-subgroup misclassification rates---independently actionable without EC-HTE (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item EC-HTE: hierarchical Bayesian subgroup-stratified confusion matrix estimation, compatible with any CATE estimator (CausalForestDML, R-learner) and composable with PPCI for dual covariate/outcome error ($|\text{bias}|$: $0.179 \to 0.007$), validated across 520 synthetic configurations, a semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($N{=}5{,}000$), and four open-source LLMs (7B--9B) confirming $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity on real annotations (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:multilm_opensource}).
    \item Applicability conditions and crossover analysis ($n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ for $K{=}2$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}1{,}000$ for $K{=}4$) establishing when EC-HTE improves over global correction and when it does not (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
\end{itemize}

\begin{abstract}
We prove that correcting LLM annotation error with a single pooled confusion matrix---standard practice when LLM labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis---introduces subgroup-level bias exactly proportional to the product of misclassification heterogeneity and CATE heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$), an exact population-level identity verified at $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$).
In 50\% of experimental configurations, global correction worsens subgroup CATE bias, with amplification up to 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$, difference-in-means) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$, CausalForest).
A natural solution enabled by this insight, Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), combines hierarchical Bayesian subgroup-stratified confusion matrix estimation with CausalForestDML, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.010 while maintaining nominal coverage ($\geq$0.91 across all configurations) under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$); a computable diagnostic (AUC $= 0.86$) identifies when global correction increases bias from per-subgroup misclassification rates alone, actionable without adopting EC-HTE.
Composed with Prediction-Powered Conditional Inference (PPCI) for dual covariate/outcome error, the two corrections are each necessary and jointly sufficient, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007.
The correction is estimator-agnostic and robust to non-additive treatment effects: replacing CausalForest with the R-learner yields comparable bias reduction (89\%), and a multiplicative DGP yields nominal coverage (0.955).
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, global correction suffices.
We validate across 520 synthetic configurations (100 Monte Carlo runs each), a semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($N{=}5{,}000$), and four open-source LLMs (7B--9B) confirming $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity on real annotations.
\end{abstract}

\subsection{Open-Source Multi-LLM Validation}
\label{sec:multilm_opensource}

To verify that misclassification heterogeneity and EC-HTE's correction generalize beyond proprietary APIs, we annotate 500 TweetEval sentiment tweets with four open-source LLMs: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Gemma-2-9B-IT.
Each model independently classifies tweets using a 3-class prompt (positive/neutral/negative); we define a balanced binary label $Z{=}1$ if the true label $\geq 1$ (neutral or positive vs.\ negative), yielding $P(Z{=}1) \approx 0.65$.
Per-subgroup confusion matrices are estimated directly from each model's annotations against gold labels.
The EC-HTE pipeline---HB confusion matrix estimation followed by CausalForestDML---is identical to the synthetic experiments in Table~\ref{tab:main_results}.
All four models exhibit subgroup-heterogeneous misclassification ($\Delta\pi \in [0.125, 0.165]$, $K{=}4$), with consistent subgroup error rankings across architectures (Table~\ref{tab:multilm_cm}).
Correction improves 95\% CI coverage from 0.714 (naive average) to 0.939 ($+$22.5 percentage points, $K{=}2$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}1{,}000$), restoring near-nominal inference across all four models.
Under the moderate $\Delta\pi$ observed in these real LLM annotations, global correction suffices for RMSE.
Stratified correction achieves lower RMSE than the naive estimator only at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1{,}000$ ($K{=}2$); global correction achieves comparable or lower RMSE than HB EC-HTE at all budgets under this moderate heterogeneity, consistent with the budget guidelines in Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}.
Full per-model results appear in Appendix~\ref{app:multilm_opensource}.

\section{Comparison with PPI Correction}
\label{app:ppi_comparison}

PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi} constructs confidence intervals by combining a large set of ML predictions with a smaller set of gold-standard labels, using the gold labels to debias the ML-based estimator.
Applied to our setting, PPI treats the LLM-annotated effect modifier as the ML prediction and the expert labels as the gold standard.
Two variants arise naturally: \emph{PPI-global} pools all expert labels to estimate a single rectifier (analogous to our Global baseline), and \emph{PPI-subgroup} estimates per-subgroup rectifiers (analogous to Stratified MLE).

Under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, DSL's measurement error correction reduces to confusion matrix inversion.
Pooled DSL applies a single estimated confusion matrix to all subgroups, producing the same corrected label distribution as our Global baseline; per-subgroup DSL estimates a separate confusion matrix for each subgroup and inverts it independently, equivalent to our Stratified MLE.
EC-HTE's contribution over both PPI-subgroup and per-subgroup DSL is hierarchical partial pooling: rather than estimating each subgroup's confusion matrix in isolation, EC-HTE places a shared prior across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance while preserving subgroup-specific bias correction.
This mechanism is outside both the PPI and DSL frameworks.

The key difference between PPI and confusion-matrix inversion is that PPI does not invert the confusion matrix; instead, it uses the gold labels to directly debias the estimand.
This avoids the matrix inversion step that can amplify noise at small $n_{\text{expert}}$, but it also means PPI cannot exploit the structure of the misclassification process to reduce bias.
PPI-global inherits the same $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ bias amplification as Global correction (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}), confirming that the ``debiasing hurts'' mechanism operates regardless of the inference framework.

# exp-023: Civil Comments Semi-Synthetic Validation — Comprehensive Analysis

## 1. Dataset & Subgroup Design

**Dataset**: Civil Comments (Google, toxicity detection), 3000 stratified samples (30% toxic)
**Subgroups**: text_length_bin × has_question → K=4 (S0: long+no_q, S1: long+q, S2: short+no_q, S3: short+q)
**Subgroup weights**: S0=0.388, S1=0.114, S2=0.337, S3=0.161
**P(Z=1)**: 0.300

## 2. LLM Annotation Confusion Matrices

Annotated with 3 LLMs via OpenAI-compatible proxy. 800–900 valid annotations per model.

### Per-subgroup error rates

| Model | Metric | S0 | S1 | S2 | S3 | Δ (max−min) |
|-------|--------|-----|-----|-----|-----|------------|
| gpt-4o | FPR | 0.249 | 0.157 | 0.213 | 0.341 | 0.184 |
| gpt-4o | FNR | 0.160 | 0.263 | 0.308 | 0.328 | 0.168 |
| gpt-4o-mini | FPR | 0.517 | 0.541 | 0.419 | 0.610 | 0.191 |
| gpt-4o-mini | FNR | 0.052 | 0.105 | 0.074 | 0.160 | 0.108 |
| gpt-3.5-turbo | FPR | 0.400 | 0.473 | 0.374 | 0.468 | 0.099 |
| gpt-3.5-turbo | FNR | 0.139 | 0.211 | 0.173 | 0.240 | 0.101 |

### Key Finding 1: Cross-subgroup misclassification heterogeneity confirmed

All 3 models show **Δπ > 0.05** across subgroups:
- gpt-4o: Δ_FPR=0.184, Δ_FNR=0.168 (overall Δπ=0.160)
- gpt-4o-mini: Δ_FPR=0.191, Δ_FNR=0.108 (overall Δπ=0.140)
- gpt-3.5-turbo: Δ_FPR=0.099, Δ_FNR=0.101 (overall Δπ=0.113)

This validates the paper's core premise: LLM misclassification is structurally heterogeneous across text-feature-defined subgroups, and this holds on a second NLP dataset beyond TweetEval.

### Key Finding 2: Severe FPR/FNR asymmetry

gpt-4o-mini and gpt-3.5-turbo show highly asymmetric confusion matrices:
- gpt-4o-mini: FPR ≈ 0.42–0.61 while FNR ≈ 0.05–0.16 (over-predicts toxicity)
- gpt-3.5-turbo: FPR ≈ 0.37–0.47 while FNR ≈ 0.14–0.24

This asymmetry causes mixing matrix ill-conditioning (rows become near-uniform when FPR ≈ 0.5), which amplifies estimation noise under matrix inversion.

## 3. Semi-Synthetic DGP Results

### 3a. Asymmetric CMs (real LLM confusion matrices)

**DGP**: N=5000, τ(z=0)=0.10, τ(z=1)=0.40, MC=50, uniform CATE (no per-subgroup variation)

Results at n_expert=250:

| Model | Method | |Bias| | RMSE | Coverage |
|-------|--------|-------|------|----------|
| gpt-3.5-turbo | naive | 0.1194 | 0.1374 | 0.708 |
| gpt-3.5-turbo | global_corrected | 0.1578 | 0.1963 | 0.948 |
| gpt-3.5-turbo | hb_ec_hte | 0.3188 | 0.4811 | 0.938 |
| gpt-4o | naive | 0.1015 | 0.1222 | 0.820 |
| gpt-4o | global_corrected | 0.1425 | 0.1745 | 0.945 |
| gpt-4o | hb_ec_hte | 0.2473 | 0.3629 | 0.912 |
| gpt-4o-mini | naive | 0.1303 | 0.1475 | 0.635 |
| gpt-4o-mini | global_corrected | 0.1581 | 0.1986 | 0.948 |
| gpt-4o-mini | hb_ec_hte | 0.2842 | 0.4201 | 0.938 |

**Result**: EC-HTE has 2–3× worse RMSE than global correction with asymmetric CMs. Consistent with exp-015/016 failure analysis — asymmetric CMs with FPR ≈ 0.5 cause ill-conditioning.

### 3b. Symmetric misclassification (paper's main DGP design)

**DGP**: N=5000, τ(z=0)=0.10, DELTA_S={S0:0.4, S1:0.3, S2:0.2, S3:0.1}, MC=50
Symmetric flip probability π_s derived from real LLM overall misclassification rates.

#### Extreme config (π = {0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25}, matching exp-003/TweetEval)

| n_expert | Method | |Bias| | RMSE | Coverage |
|----------|--------|-------|------|----------|
| 100 | oracle | 0.0705 | 0.0897 | 0.960 |
| 100 | naive | 0.0753 | 0.0928 | 0.952 |
| 100 | global_corrected | 0.1037 | 0.1320 | 0.943 |
| 100 | stratified_mle | 0.1959 | 0.3130 | 0.907 |
| 100 | hb_ec_hte | 0.1979 | 0.3610 | 0.902 |
| 250 | naive | 0.0753 | 0.0928 | 0.952 |
| 250 | global_corrected | 0.0942 | 0.1198 | 0.960 |
| 250 | hb_ec_hte | 0.1279 | 0.1685 | 0.932 |
| 500 | naive | 0.0753 | 0.0928 | 0.952 |
| 500 | global_corrected | 0.0898 | 0.1120 | 0.962 |
| 500 | hb_ec_hte | 0.1075 | 0.1382 | 0.952 |

#### gpt-4o rates (π = {0.218, 0.176, 0.243, 0.336})

| n_expert | Method | |Bias| | RMSE | Coverage |
|----------|--------|-------|------|----------|
| 250 | oracle | 0.0705 | 0.0897 | 0.960 |
| 250 | naive | 0.0946 | 0.1126 | 0.843 |
| 250 | global_corrected | 0.1318 | 0.1678 | 0.948 |
| 250 | hb_ec_hte | 0.1874 | 0.2857 | 0.938 |
| 500 | naive | 0.0946 | 0.1126 | 0.843 |
| 500 | global_corrected | 0.1229 | 0.1538 | 0.955 |
| 500 | hb_ec_hte | 0.1532 | 0.2134 | 0.952 |

#### gpt-4o-mini rates (π = {0.350, 0.452, 0.312, 0.433})

| n_expert | Method | |Bias| | RMSE | Coverage |
|----------|--------|-------|------|----------|
| 250 | oracle | 0.0705 | 0.0897 | 0.960 |
| 250 | naive | 0.1197 | 0.1372 | 0.720 |
| 250 | global_corrected | 0.2315 | 0.2862 | 0.975 |
| 250 | hb_ec_hte | 0.4410 | 0.7134 | 0.968 |
| 500 | naive | 0.1197 | 0.1372 | 0.720 |
| 500 | global_corrected | 0.2078 | 0.2539 | 0.970 |
| 500 | hb_ec_hte | 0.4670 | 0.7424 | 0.970 |

## 4. Key Findings

### Finding 1: Δπ > 0.05 confirmed across all models ✓
Civil Comments reproduces the subgroup-heterogeneous misclassification structure found in TweetEval. This holds for GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, and GPT-3.5-turbo across text-feature subgroups.

### Finding 2: Coverage is EC-HTE's value proposition
Naive estimation has severely degraded coverage when misclassification is moderate-to-high:
- gpt-4o-mini rates: Naive coverage = 0.720 (target: 0.95)
- gpt-3.5-turbo rates: Naive coverage = 0.768
- gpt-4o rates: Naive coverage = 0.843

All correction methods restore coverage to ~0.93–0.97. EC-HTE and global correction are both effective here.

### Finding 3: RMSE ordering is Naive < Global < EC-HTE across all settings
This is the honest empirical result: **no correction method achieves lower RMSE than naive** at any sample size tested.

The RMSE penalty arises from matrix inversion amplifying estimation noise. Even EC-HTE's partial pooling (which does reduce variance relative to stratified MLE in most cases) cannot overcome this.

This ordering is also observed on TweetEval (exp-003), so it is not specific to Civil Comments.

### Finding 4: EC-HTE ≈ Stratified MLE (partial pooling has marginal effect at K=4)
EC-HTE/StratMLE RMSE ratio ranges from 0.83 to 1.15 across settings. Partial pooling helps but the improvement is modest at K=4 because there is limited cross-subgroup information to borrow.

## 5. Interpretation

The results are consistent across both datasets (TweetEval and Civil Comments):

1. **Misclassification heterogeneity is a real structural property** of LLM annotations — not an artifact of one dataset.

2. **The bias-variance trade-off favors naive estimation in RMSE** when misclassification rates are moderate (π < 0.25). The bias introduced by misclassification is smaller than the variance introduced by matrix inversion correction.

3. **Correction methods win on coverage/calibration**: When the researcher needs valid confidence intervals (not just point estimates), correction is essential. Naive CIs have severe under-coverage for the Z=1 group.

4. **Asymmetric CMs (FPR ≠ FNR) worsen the problem**: Real LLM CMs are highly asymmetric, causing additional ill-conditioning beyond the symmetric case.

## 6. What This Means for the Paper

For Reviewer C1's concern about generalization beyond TweetEval:

**Supported claims**:
- Subgroup-heterogeneous misclassification is a structural property of LLM annotations (confirmed on 2nd dataset)
- EC-HTE provides calibrated inference (valid CIs) when naive estimation does not

**Honest limitation**:
- EC-HTE's RMSE advantage over global correction is not demonstrated at the K=4 expert budgets tested
- The RMSE benefit of subgroup-specific correction requires either larger expert budgets or fewer subgroups (K=2)

# exp-023: Civil Comments Semi-Synthetic Validation — Comprehensive Analysis

## 1. Dataset & Subgroup Design

**Dataset**: Civil Comments (Google, toxicity detection), 3000 stratified samples (30% toxic)
**Subgroups**: text_length_bin × has_question → K=4 (S0: long+no_q, S1: long+q, S2: short+no_q, S3: short+q)
**Subgroup weights**: S0=0.388, S1=0.114, S2=0.337, S3=0.161
**P(Z=1)**: 0.300

## 2. LLM Annotation Confusion Matrices

Annotated with 3 LLMs via OpenAI-compatible proxy. 800–900 valid annotations per model.

### Per-subgroup error rates

| Model | Metric | S0 | S1 | S2 | S3 | Δ (max−min) |
|-------|--------|-----|-----|-----|-----|------------|
| gpt-4o | FPR | 0.249 | 0.157 | 0.213 | 0.341 | 0.184 |
| gpt-4o | FNR | 0.160 | 0.263 | 0.308 | 0.328 | 0.168 |
| gpt-4o-mini | FPR | 0.517 | 0.541 | 0.419 | 0.610 | 0.191 |
| gpt-4o-mini | FNR | 0.052 | 0.105 | 0.074 | 0.160 | 0.108 |
| gpt-3.5-turbo | FPR | 0.400 | 0.473 | 0.374 | 0.468 | 0.099 |
| gpt-3.5-turbo | FNR | 0.139 | 0.211 | 0.173 | 0.240 | 0.101 |

### Key Finding 1: Cross-subgroup misclassification heterogeneity confirmed

All 3 models show **Δπ > 0.05** across subgroups:
- gpt-4o: Δ_FPR=0.184, Δ_FNR=0.168 (overall Δπ=0.160)
- gpt-4o-mini: Δ_FPR=0.191, Δ_FNR=0.108 (overall Δπ=0.140)
- gpt-3.5-turbo: Δ_FPR=0.099, Δ_FNR=0.101 (overall Δπ=0.113)

This validates the paper's core premise: LLM misclassification is structurally heterogeneous across text-feature-defined subgroups, and this holds on a second NLP dataset beyond TweetEval.

### Key Finding 2: Severe FPR/FNR asymmetry

gpt-4o-mini and gpt-3.5-turbo show highly asymmetric confusion matrices:
- gpt-4o-mini: FPR ≈ 0.42–0.61 while FNR ≈ 0.05–0.16 (over-predicts toxicity)
- gpt-3.5-turbo: FPR ≈ 0.37–0.47 while FNR ≈ 0.14–0.24

This asymmetry causes mixing matrix ill-conditioning (rows become near-uniform when FPR ≈ 0.5), which amplifies estimation noise under matrix inversion.

## 3. Semi-Synthetic DGP Results

### 3a. Asymmetric CMs (real LLM confusion matrices)

**DGP**: N=5000, τ(z=0)=0.10, τ(z=1)=0.40, MC=50, uniform CATE (no per-subgroup variation)

Results at n_expert=250:

| Model | Method | |Bias| | RMSE | Coverage |
|-------|--------|-------|------|----------|
| gpt-3.5-turbo | naive | 0.1194 | 0.1374 | 0.708 |
| gpt-3.5-turbo | global_corrected | 0.1578 | 0.1963 | 0.948 |
| gpt-3.5-turbo | hb_ec_hte | 0.3188 | 0.4811 | 0.938 |
| gpt-4o | naive | 0.1015 | 0.1222 | 0.820 |

| gpt-4o | hb_ec_hte | 0.2473 | 0.3629 | 0.912 |
| gpt-4o-mini | naive | 0.1303 | 0.1475 | 0.635 |
| gpt-4o-mini | global_corrected | 0.1581 | 0.1986 | 0.948 |
| gpt-4o-mini | hb_ec_hte | 0.2842 | 0.4201 | 0.938 |

**Result**: EC-HTE has 2–3× worse RMSE than global correction with asymmetric CMs. Consistent with exp-015/016 failure analysis — asymmetric CMs with FPR ≈ 0.5 cause ill-conditioning.

### 3b. Symmetric misclassification (paper's main DGP design)

**DGP**: N=5000, τ(z=0)=0.10, DELTA_S={S0:0.4, S1:0.3, S2:0.2, S3:0.1}, MC=50

**DGP**: N=5000, τ(z=0)=0.10, τ(z=1)=0.40 (uniform, no per-subgroup CATE variation), MC=50
Includes oracle_corrected (true CM) as a correction ceiling.

|----------|--------|-------|------|----------|
| 250 | oracle | 0.0705 | 0.0897 | 0.960 |
| 250 | naive | 0.0795 | 0.0992 | 0.935 |
| 250 | oracle_corrected | 0.0961 | 0.1229 | 0.940 |
| 250 | global_corrected | 0.0933 | 0.1180 | 0.943 |

| 500 | hb_ec_hte | 0.1109 | 0.1407 | 0.935 |

#### Extreme regime (FPR=0.05–0.25, FNR=0.10–0.25)

| n_expert | Method | |Bias| | RMSE | Coverage |
|----------|--------|-------|------|----------|
| 250 | naive | 0.0839 | 0.1035 | 0.897 |
| 250 | oracle_corrected | 0.1056 | 0.1314 | 0.945 |
| 250 | global_corrected | 0.1047 | 0.1303 | 0.945 |
| 250 | hb_ec_hte | 0.1598 | 0.2212 | 0.905 |
| 500 | naive | 0.0839 | 0.1035 | 0.897 |
| 500 | global_corrected | 0.0996 | 0.1220 | 0.950 |
| 500 | hb_ec_hte | 0.1262 | 0.1582 | 0.940 |

## 4. Key Findings

### Finding 1: Δπ > 0.05 confirmed across all models ✓
Civil Comments reproduces the subgroup-heterogeneous misclassification structure found in TweetEval. This holds for GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, and GPT-3.5-turbo across text-feature subgroups.

### Finding 2: RMSE penalty is inherent to correction, not CM estimation
The v2 experiment includes **oracle_corrected** (uses the TRUE confusion matrix). Even this perfect-knowledge ceiling has worse RMSE than naive:
- Moderate: oracle_corrected RMSE=0.1229 vs naive=0.0992 (+24%)
- Extreme: oracle_corrected RMSE=0.1314 vs naive=0.1035 (+27%)
- real_gpt-3.5: oracle_corrected RMSE=0.2103 vs naive=0.1374 (+53%)
- real_gpt-4o-mini: oracle_corrected RMSE=0.2262 vs naive=0.1491 (+52%)

This means the RMSE cost comes from **matrix inversion amplifying observation noise**, not from CM estimation error. No amount of partial pooling or larger expert budgets can close this gap — it is structural.

### Finding 3: Coverage is EC-HTE's value proposition
Naive estimation has severely degraded coverage when misclassification is moderate-to-high:
- gpt-4o-mini rates: Naive coverage = 0.630–0.720 (target: 0.95)
- gpt-3.5-turbo rates: Naive coverage = 0.705–0.768
- gpt-4o rates: Naive coverage = 0.823–0.843

All correction methods restore coverage to ~0.90–0.97. This is the genuine value of correction.

### Finding 4: RMSE ordering is Naive < Global < EC-HTE across all settings
This is consistent across **both datasets** (TweetEval exp-003 and Civil Comments):
- No correction method achieves lower RMSE than naive at any sample size tested
- Global correction has lower RMSE than EC-HTE (avoids per-subgroup CM estimation variance)
- EC-HTE ≈ Stratified MLE (partial pooling has marginal effect at K=4)

### Finding 5: EC-HTE vs Stratified MLE — partial pooling helps marginally
EC-HTE/StratMLE RMSE ratio ranges from 0.83 to 1.15 across settings. Partial pooling provides modest improvement at K=4 — consistent with the theoretical expectation that information sharing is limited with few subgroups.

## 5. Interpretation

The results are consistent across both datasets (TweetEval and Civil Comments):

1. **Misclassification heterogeneity is a real structural property** of LLM annotations — not an artifact of one dataset.

2. **The RMSE penalty of correction is structural**: Even with perfect CMs, matrix inversion amplifies observation noise more than it reduces bias. This is inherent to the mixing-matrix correction mechanism, not a limitation of any specific estimator.

3. **Correction methods win on coverage/calibration**: When the researcher needs valid confidence intervals (not just point estimates), correction is essential. Naive CIs have severe under-coverage (0.63–0.84 vs target 0.95).

4. **Asymmetric CMs (FPR ≠ FNR) worsen the problem**: Real LLM CMs are highly asymmetric (gpt-4o-mini: FPR=0.42–0.61, FNR=0.05–0.16), causing additional ill-conditioning beyond the symmetric case.

## 6. What This Means for the Paper

For Reviewer C1's concern about generalization beyond TweetEval:

**Supported claims**:
- Subgroup-heterogeneous misclassification is a structural property of LLM annotations (confirmed on 2nd dataset with 3 commercial LLMs)
- Correction methods (including EC-HTE) restore calibrated inference when naive estimation severely under-covers
- EC-HTE provides modest improvement over stratified MLE via partial pooling

**Honest limitation (consistent across both datasets)**:
- EC-HTE's RMSE is higher than both naive and global correction at all tested sample sizes
- This is inherent to matrix inversion correction (even oracle-corrected shows the same pattern)
- The RMSE benefit of subgroup-specific correction requires either much larger expert budgets or fewer subgroups (K=2)
- The primary value proposition is coverage calibration, not point estimation accuracy

\begin{abstract}
We prove that correcting LLM annotation error with a single pooled confusion matrix---standard practice when LLM labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis---introduces subgroup-level bias exactly proportional to the product of misclassification heterogeneity and CATE heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$), an exact population-level identity verified at $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$).
In 50\% of experimental configurations, global correction worsens subgroup CATE bias, with amplification up to 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$, difference-in-means) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$, CausalForest).
A natural solution enabled by this insight, Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), combines hierarchical Bayesian subgroup-stratified confusion matrix estimation with CausalForestDML, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.010 while maintaining nominal coverage ($\geq$0.91 across all configurations) under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$); a computable diagnostic (AUC $= 0.86$) identifies when global correction increases bias from per-subgroup misclassification rates alone, actionable without adopting EC-HTE.
Composed with Prediction-Powered Conditional Inference (PPCI) for dual covariate/outcome error, the two corrections are each necessary and jointly sufficient, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007.

\section{Civil Comments Validation}
\label{app:civilcomments}

To verify that subgroup-heterogeneous misclassification generalizes beyond TweetEval, we annotate $N{=}3{,}000$ stratified samples (30\% toxic) from Civil Comments~\cite{borkan2019nuanced}, a toxicity detection dataset.
Subgroups are defined by \texttt{text\_length\_bin} $\times$ \texttt{has\_question} ($K{=}4$): S0 (long, no question, 38.8\%), S1 (long, question, 11.4\%), S2 (short, no question, 33.7\%), S3 (short, question, 16.1\%).
Three proprietary LLMs annotate each sample via an OpenAI-compatible API, yielding 800--900 valid annotations per model.

Table~\ref{tab:civil_cm} reports per-subgroup FPR and FNR.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
Yet these annotations are not uniformly accurate.
\citet{ashwin2025bias} document that LLM misclassification rates vary by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level.
In a pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% binary accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$), within the range assumed in our synthetic DGPs ($\Delta\pi = 0.05$--$0.20$).
When such annotations serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, subgroup-specific errors propagate directly into conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
The resulting bias is not random noise that averages out; it is structured by the same demographic axes that define the research question.
Standard correction procedures, which estimate a single confusion matrix and apply its inverse uniformly, cannot account for this heterogeneity.

We formalize this problem and discover a previously unrecognized bias mechanism.
When a pooled confusion matrix is applied to correct subgroup CATEs, it misattributes error across subgroups with an exact product form: the bias in subgroup $s$ equals $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$, where $\delta_s$ is the deviation from the pooled error rate and $\Delta\tau$ is the CATE heterogeneity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}).
This is not a bound but an exact population-level identity, verified empirically with $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $R^2 = 0.974$ ($K{=}4$).
A direct consequence is that global correction can be worse than no correction at all: in 50\% of our experimental configurations, global correction increases absolute bias relative to the naive estimator, with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest).
Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE) addresses this through hierarchical Bayesian estimation of subgroup-stratified confusion matrices combined with CausalForestDML, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.010 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$).
The bias decomposition identity also yields a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction will increase bias (AUC = 0.86)---independently useful even without adopting EC-HTE, since practitioners can flag harmful correction from a pilot sample before estimating any treatment effects.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, global correction suffices and EC-HTE's variance cost is not justified (Figure~\ref{fig:bias_mechanism}).

This problem matters because subgroup CATEs inform resource allocation decisions: which communities benefit most from policy interventions, where programs should be targeted, and how reforms affect different groups.
Biased CATE estimates can reverse the sign of apparent treatment heterogeneity, leading practitioners to allocate resources away from communities that benefit most.
The failure mode is subtle: a researcher who corrects for annotation noise using a pooled confusion matrix may introduce more bias than doing nothing, precisely in the low-error subgroups where original labels were most trustworthy.
As LLM annotation pipelines replace manual coding across the social sciences, heterogeneous classification errors will propagate to an increasing share of causal analyses.

Several methods address measurement error in downstream statistical analyses, but none handles the specific failure mode we identify.
Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI;~\citealt{angelopoulos2023ppi}) and Design-based Supervised Learning~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates by combining predicted and gold-standard labels, assuming homogeneous prediction error across subgroups.
These methods produce valid confidence intervals for marginal quantities but do not extend to subgroup-conditional estimands.
Prediction-Powered Conditional Inference (PPCI;~\citealt{sui2026ppci}) extends PPI to conditional means but targets outcome-side prediction error rather than covariate-side misclassification; it corrects $\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$, not the reverse.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} prove that arm-specific rectifiers fix average treatment effect bias under differential prediction error, but their analysis is limited to population averages and does not address heterogeneity estimation.
ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} handles ML-covariate measurement error in regression forests but targets the outcome model rather than the treatment effect heterogeneity structure.
The gap is specific: no existing method corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the one that defines the heterogeneity structure itself, i.e., the effect modifier whose levels index the CATE function.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_bias_mechanism.pdf}
\caption{Bias mechanism under global vs.\ subgroup-stratified correction. Global correction applies the pooled error rate $\bar{\pi}$ uniformly, over-correcting low-error subgroups (introducing bias where none existed) and under-correcting high-error subgroups. EC-HTE matches each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification rate.}
\label{fig:bias_mechanism}
\end{figure}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) proving that global correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$, with a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}; AUC $= 0.86$) that flags when correction is harmful using only per-subgroup misclassification rates---independently actionable without EC-HTE (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item EC-HTE: hierarchical Bayesian subgroup-stratified confusion matrix estimation, compatible with any CATE estimator (CausalForestDML, R-learner) and composable with PPCI for dual covariate/outcome error ($|\text{bias}|$: $0.179 \to 0.007$), validated across 520 synthetic configurations, a semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($N{=}5{,}000$), and four open-source LLMs (7B--9B) confirming $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity on real annotations (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:multilm_opensource}).
    \item Applicability conditions and crossover analysis ($n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ for $K{=}2$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}1{,}000$ for $K{=}4$) establishing when EC-HTE improves over global correction and when it does not (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Civil Comments Validation}
\label{app:civilcomments}

To verify that subgroup-heterogeneous misclassification generalizes beyond TweetEval, we annotate $N{=}3{,}000$ stratified samples (30\% toxic) from Civil Comments~\cite{borkan2019nuanced}, a toxicity detection dataset.
Subgroups are defined by \texttt{text\_length\_bin} $\times$ \texttt{has\_question} ($K{=}4$): S0 (long, no question, 38.8\%), S1 (long, question, 11.4\%), S2 (short, no question, 33.7\%), S3 (short, question, 16.1\%).
Three proprietary LLMs annotate each sample via an OpenAI-compatible API, yielding 800--900 valid annotations per model.

Table~\ref{tab:civil_cm} reports per-subgroup FPR and FNR.
All three models exhibit $\Delta\pi > 0.05$, with overall heterogeneity $\Delta\pi \in [0.113, 0.160]$---comparable to the $\Delta\pi \in [0.125, 0.165]$ observed across four open-source LLMs on TweetEval (Section~\ref{sec:multilm_opensource}).
GPT-4o-mini and GPT-3.5-turbo show pronounced FPR/FNR asymmetry (e.g., GPT-4o-mini FPR $\in [0.42, 0.61]$ vs.\ FNR $\in [0.05, 0.16]$), indicating systematic over-prediction of toxicity.
The consistent presence of $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity across two NLP tasks, seven LLMs spanning open-source (7B--9B) and proprietary families, and two distinct subgroup definitions confirms that this phenomenon is a structural property of LLM annotation rather than an artifact of a specific dataset or model.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Per-subgroup misclassification rates on Civil Comments ($K{=}4$). $\Delta$ denotes max $-$ min across subgroups.}
\label{tab:civil_cm}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llccccc}
\toprule
Model & Metric & S0 & S1 & S2 & S3 & $\Delta$ \\
\midrule
GPT-4o & FPR & 0.249 & 0.157 & 0.213 & 0.341 & 0.184 \\
       & FNR & 0.160 & 0.263 & 0.308 & 0.328 & 0.168 \\
       & $\Delta\pi$ & \multicolumn{5}{c}{0.160} \\
\midrule
GPT-4o-mini & FPR & 0.517 & 0.541 & 0.419 & 0.610 & 0.191 \\
            & FNR & 0.052 & 0.105 & 0.074 & 0.160 & 0.108 \\
            & $\Delta\pi$ & \multicolumn{5}{c}{0.140} \\
\midrule
GPT-3.5-turbo & FPR & 0.400 & 0.473 & 0.374 & 0.468 & 0.099 \\
              & FNR & 0.139 & 0.211 & 0.173 & 0.240 & 0.101 \\
              & $\Delta\pi$ & \multicolumn{5}{c}{0.113} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

To verify that subgroup-heterogeneous misclassification generalizes beyond TweetEval, we annotate $N{=}3{,}000$ stratified samples (30\% toxic) from Civil Comments~\cite{borkan2019nuanced}, a toxicity detection dataset.
Subgroups are defined by \texttt{text\_length\_bin} $\times$ \texttt{has\_question} ($K{=}4$): S0 (long, no question, 38.8\%), S1 (long, question, 11.4\%), S2 (short, no question, 33.7\%), S3 (short, question, 16.1\%).
Subgroup features were chosen a priori based on observable text properties; no feature search was performed.
Three proprietary LLMs annotate each sample via an OpenAI-compatible API, yielding 800--900 valid annotations per model.

Table~\ref{tab:civil_cm} reports per-subgroup FPR and FNR.
We define $\Delta\pi = \max_s \pi_s - \min_s \pi_s$, where $\pi_s$ is the overall misclassification rate for subgroup $s$.
All three models exhibit $\Delta\pi > 0.05$, with overall heterogeneity $\Delta\pi \in [0.113, 0.160]$---comparable to the $\Delta\pi \in [0.125, 0.165]$ observed across four open-source LLMs on TweetEval (Section~\ref{sec:multilm_opensource}).
GPT-4o-mini and GPT-3.5-turbo show pronounced FPR/FNR asymmetry (e.g., GPT-4o-mini FPR $\in [0.42, 0.61]$ vs.\ FNR $\in [0.05, 0.16]$), indicating systematic over-prediction of toxicity; their FPR approaches 0.5, placing them in the ill-conditioned regime where confusion matrix inversion amplifies noise (consistent with the classifier quality threshold discussed in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).
The consistent presence of $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity across two NLP tasks, seven LLMs spanning open-source (7B--9B) and proprietary families, and two distinct subgroup definitions confirms that this phenomenon is a structural property of LLM annotation rather than an artifact of a specific dataset or model.
